name: Bianca Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer the late billing calls at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and am still learning the job; a reversed payment can send me to ask the agent beside me which date is final. The late shift pays better than most agent shifts. I do not use AI tools, and I want a human to read the account before saying a bill is settled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo keeps a museum building open, and our children are grown and living independently. We have around nine months of expenses saved. Several centres nearby advertise similar work, though another night rota would have to make sense for both of us. I like ending a call with a corrected balance, not a promise that someone else will call back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau is no reason to rush a wrong-bill call. I would bring the staff group a case where the customer had to ring twice because a payment was marked settled too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my late hours and pay will hold. Jo and I have nine months put aside and several other centres nearby, so this small change does not threaten our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking late billing calls and bring two reopened balances to the monthly staff meeting. In the first year of this mild change, I’d sign the group request for paid correction minutes before a bill is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money, impatient with a target that hides a wrong balance. The customer does not live inside the call-count chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One payment had been moved to the wrong account with the same surname. The agent had to open it again because the first call was timed too tightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change household savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (my partner) and I would leave our nine-month reserve in place for household repairs. We have no reason to spend it to celebrate a faster script.

say: I’d ask colleagues for **paid correction minutes** before closing bills.
I’d show **reopened balances** hidden by the call-count target.
think: I think my **late-shift pay** remains secure in this picture.
I trust our **nine-month reserve** and nearby jobs for ordinary setbacks.
do: Keep **taking late billing calls** and present two reopened cases at the staff meeting.
Sign the group’s **paid correction request** in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about wages, impatient with bad targets.
S0.quote: The customer does not live inside the call-count chart.
fieldNote: Her **higher late-shift pay** and strong reserve calm immediate money worries.
The **group request** seeks paid correction time for workers.
Existing savings are **retained**, not newly built.

steps.text: Keep handling late billing calls and show two reopened cases at staff meeting
Sign staff request for paid correction minutes before bill closure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will clear the plain balance questions first and leave the calls where the ledger and the customer disagree. I would ask other agents to sign for a paid human appeal rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could still learn the hard billing cases, but the centre might need fewer late agents. Nine months saved means Jo and I need not accept the first offer, though I do not want the next agent’s shift erased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join the agents’ written demand for paid appeal hours and keep practising disputed balances with an experienced coworker on my shift. In the first year routine calls move, I’d ask for the new late rota in writing and continue paid calls while it still has hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about fewer shifts, though we have room to respond. A long reserve does not make a missing wage a good bargain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the appeal rota track?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count how many disputed balances return after an automated answer. The appeal rota should grow if those cases grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change centres yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (my partner) and I would compare next month’s paid hours with the household bills. I would not leave for another centre merely because it has a newer title.

say: I’d join agents demanding a **paid appeal rota** for disputed bills.
I’d show **repeat balances** after automated answers.
think: I think I could learn **harder billing cases** from the experienced agents on my shift.
I worry **fewer late shifts** may follow easy-call automation.
do: Join agents’ **written appeal-hours demand** and keep practising disputed balances in 2026.
Request **written late rota** in the first year and keep paid calls while hours remain.
feel: **Anxious** about shifts, with time to respond.
S1.quote: A long reserve does not make a missing wage a good bargain.
fieldNote: Her **nine-month reserve** allows negotiation but cannot replace ongoing wages.
She makes a **shared worker demand** for paid appeal hours.
Current-job practice is **keep-going**, not a new trade or AI learning.

steps.text: Join agents’ written demand for paid human appeal hours
Keep practising disputed balances on paid shifts and request written late rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AGI by 2028 could read a bill, decide the dispute and answer the caller. Robots around 2031 are later; the late headset wage is at risk first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could remove a large part of my paid week. Nine months saved gives us search time, and there are local centres, but Jo’s museum wage alone is not a replacement for mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues asking for written cut dates and a paid route to challenge wrong AI decisions. If my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid billing job at a nearby centre after checking written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel; I’d keep my present shift until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible loss of a paid week. Savings buy time; they do not give a machine the right to mark a wrong bill final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real appeal allow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who has permission to reverse a charge after the software says no. If there is only a complaint form, the customer is still waiting for a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jo check in an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (my partner) would check whether another centre’s late rota still lets us get home safely. We would compare the whole week of pay, including the journey, before I signed anything.

say: I’d seek **written cut dates** and paid appeals with colleagues.
I’d say **2028 thinking AI** threatens the late headset before robots.
think: I think my **paid week** could shrink sharply.
I know **nine months saved** buys search time, not another wage.
do: Join colleagues’ **notice and appeal demand** in 2026.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid billing** with written bill-covering net pay/hours and safe journey; stay until signed offer.
S2.quote: Savings buy time; they do not give a machine the right to mark a wrong bill final.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** buys search time despite possible wage loss.
The group asks for **reversal authority**, beyond a general complaint form.
A move needs **written whole-week net pay**, safe travel and a signed offer.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written cut dates and paid human appeal authority
Apply for nearby posted paid billing with written bill-covering net pay/hours, safe travel; move when signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives our centre years to keep paid correction work in the staffing plan. I would press the staff group to renew its appeal-hours request each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might stay on difficult bills for a while, though full thinking AI could read those too in 2031. There are several centres nearby, and I would look at a real paid appeals role before changing my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep the late billing shift and bring reopened-case numbers to the yearly staff request for appeal hours. In the first year after 2031, if my hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid appeals post only after checking written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel; I would leave only on a signed offer with a safe journey home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer warning lets us bargain over real hours. A five-year plan should name the people paid to reverse mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would you inspect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask an appeals agent whether they can change the account or must forward a note. I would not take a new title if the authority disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the journey cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo (my partner) would check the last bus for a different late shift. An extra hour of pay means little if I have to buy an expensive ride home.

say: I’d renew the **paid appeal-hours request** with coworkers every year until management posts real shifts.
I’d demand **account correction authority** in any appeals post.
think: I think I may keep **difficult billing work** for a time.
I know **2031 AGI** may still read those disputes.
do: Keep **paid late billing calls** and join annual appeal-hours requests with case counts.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid appeals** with correction authority, written net bill-covering weekly pay/hours and last bus; move when signed.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to bargain over staffing.
S3.quote: A five-year plan should name the people paid to reverse mistakes.
fieldNote: The **annual worker demand** uses reopened-case evidence.
She checks **real appeal authority**, not a grander job title.
A signed offer needs **net weekly pay** and last-bus travel.

steps.text: Keep handling paid late billing calls
Join yearly staff request for paid appeal hours using reopened-case counts
Apply for posted appeals with correction authority, written bill-covering net pay/hours, last bus; move when signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to keep correction authority in paid hands. I would ask the staff group to put paid appeal hours in each yearly rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be retired by 68, but Jo and I have not checked the income that would replace both wages. Full thinking AI could still end billing calls in 2036; robots around 2039 do not delay that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep my paid late shifts and ask Jo to compare verified later-life income with our bills before we set any stopping date. If I still need wages after 2036 and my call hours fall, I’d apply for posted paid account work nearby and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, steady enough today to check it. I will not promise retirement from the size of a savings account alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would staff compare each spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a copy of our paid hours beside the number of customer reversals each spring. If hours fall while wrong balances rise, staff have a clear request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our adult children have their own work. Jo (my partner) and I would not assume they could carry us; we can ask them for advice without putting their wages in our plan.

I’d keep **customer reversals** beside staffing numbers.
think: I think I **might retire by 68** if verified income permits.
I know **2036 AGI** could still remove billing calls.
do: Keep **paid late shifts** and compare verified later-life income with bills before any retirement date.
Join the group’s **yearly appeal-hours request** using reversal counts.
Seek **posted account work** if wages remain needed after cuts; move only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about the endpoint, steady enough now to check.

fieldNote: Her **nine-month savings** do not establish retirement income.
The group connects **paid appeal hours** with actual reversals.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could settle the billing calls and remove my late-shift wage, even if I am still learning the work. Nine months saved and other local centres give us time to search, but I would want written notice and paid human authority to reverse a wrong bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: When a payment is wrong, the customer needs a correction, not another cheerful answer. The right to appeal needs someone on a paid rota who can change the account.

headlineQuote: The right to appeal needs someone on a paid rota who can change the account.
portrait: At **58**, Bianca is a junior late-shift billing agent still learning after secondary school.
She and Jo have **grown children**, higher pay and about nine months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and prefers direct account checks by paid staff.
Several **nearby centres** give her options, while she presses for human correction authority.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the late-shift wage she depends on.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and paid human appeal authority for wrong bills would help.
